name: Methadone (Dolophine, Methadose)
summary: Long-acting opioid agonist used to treat opioid use disorder (OUD). It reduces withdrawal and cravings, but carries serious overdose and heart-rhythm risks—especially early in treatment and when mixed with sedatives.
description: Methadone is a long-acting opioid medicine used in structured programs to treat opioid use disorder. At the right dose, it stops withdrawal, quiets cravings, and blocks the “high” from other opioids. It can also slow breathing and, in some people, prolong the QT interval (a heart rhythm risk), especially during dose changes. Mixing methadone with alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, or other sedatives can be fatal. Dosing must be individualized and increased slowly because methadone builds up over several days.
patient_summary: Methadone is a long-acting opioid medicine used in structured programs to treat opioid use disorder. At the right dose, it stops withdrawal, quiets cravings, and blocks the “high” from other opioids. It can also slow breathing and, in some people, prolong the QT interval (a heart rhythm risk), especially during dose changes. Mixing methadone with alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, or other sedatives can be fatal. Dosing must be individualized and increased slowly because methadone builds up over several days.

linked_conditions.context: Methadone is a core medication treatment for OUD. The goal isn’t to “snow” someone—it’s to hold them steady: no withdrawal, no cravings, and less reinforcement from other opioids.
Methadone can be used short-term to stabilize opioid withdrawal, but outcomes are generally better with ongoing maintenance treatment when appropriate.

When opioid withdrawal is driving anxiety, agitation, and insomnia, treating the withdrawal can dramatically improve those symptoms. Methadone doesn’t treat primary anxiety disorders—it treats opioid physiology.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to methadone or any component of the formulation
Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Varies by dose, tolerance, and treatment setting
efficacy_response.patient_text: When methadone dosing is done carefully and monitored closely, many people feel a very clear shift: withdrawal calms down, cravings get quieter, and daily life becomes more manageable. The dose has to be individualized and increased slowly because methadone accumulates over the first several days.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well-absorbed orally with highly variable bioavailability
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral: ~0.5 to 1 hour (analgesic onset); stabilization effects may evolve over the first several days as levels accumulate
pharmacokinetics.half_life: 8 to 59 hours (may be longer in hepatic impairment; changes during early treatment can occur due to auto-induction in some patients)
pharmacokinetics.duration_oral: Craving suppression: ~24 to 36 hours; early analgesic duration may be shorter than respiratory depressant effects
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (primarily CYP3A4, CYP2B6; also CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6) to inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (<10% unchanged); excretion increases with acidic urine; tissue storage can prolong effect

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Methadone is primarily used in structured, closely monitored treatment to manage {link:condition:opioid-use-disorder:opioid use disorder (OUD)}. In the right setting and dose, it prevents withdrawal, reduces cravings, and lowers the pull of other opioids by building steady opioid receptor coverage. It is not an “as-needed” medication, and it’s not a casual prescription—methadone is powerful, long-lasting, and requires careful titration and monitoring.
items: {link:condition:opioid-use-disorder:Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) maintenance treatment}: Prevents withdrawal, reduces cravings, and supports long-term recovery stability
{link:condition:opioid-withdrawal:Opioid withdrawal (short-term, medically supervised)}: Stabilizes withdrawal when short-term detox is chosen (though maintenance often has better outcomes)
off_label: Withdrawal prevention and opioid weaning support in hospitalized/ICU settings (adjunctive use to reduce continuous opioid infusion and reduce withdrawal-driven agitation)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s experience is different, but these are common themes people report when methadone is started and dosed carefully:

items.category: Withdrawal Relief (first 1-4 hours, then steadier over days)
quotes: It wasn’t a high. It was just… normal. Like my body stopped screaming.
I could sit still again. The crawling-out-of-my-skin feeling eased up.
I didn’t realize how much of my “anxiety” was withdrawal until it quieted.
items.note: Methadone can start helping the same day, but full steady-state effects build over 3 to 5 days on a dose.

quotes: The obsession dial turned down. I still had thoughts, but it wasn’t controlling me.
I could make decisions without panic-driving everything.
I finally had space to work on the rest of my life.
The first few days I felt heavy and sleepy.
I nodded off in the afternoon and realized my dose might be too high.
I felt calm, but also kind of foggy at first.
items.note: Sedation can be a warning sign, especially 2 to 4 hours after dosing. It can mean the dose is too high, the titration is too fast, or there’s a dangerous interaction.

items.category: If You Miss Doses, Your Body Notices
quotes: If I missed a dose, I didn’t just feel anxious—I felt sick and wired.
The chills, stomach stuff, and insomnia hit like a wave.
I thought I was fine, then day two felt brutal.
items.note: Withdrawal can be delayed compared to short-acting opioids and can last longer.

items.category: The Logistics and the Stigma (real-world experience)
quotes: The clinic routine was annoying at first, but it also kept me accountable.
I hated the stigma—until I started functioning again.
It’s hard, but stability is worth it.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Methadone can start easing withdrawal the day you take it, but it’s not a “one-and-done” medication. It builds up in the body over several days, which is exactly why dosing has to be slow and careful.
key_points: 0.5 to 1 hour: Oral effects can begin (especially for withdrawal discomfort)
1 to 7.5 hours: Peak blood levels (timing varies a lot person to person)
3 to 5 days: Full steady-state effect on a given dose (methadone accumulates)
24 to 36 hours: Typical craving suppression window at a stable dose (varies)
Respiratory depression can peak later and last longer than “how it feels,” especially early in treatment

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Methadone’s effectiveness is about stability: no withdrawal, reduced cravings, and less reinforcement from other opioids. The key is individualized dosing and slow titration—methadone can feel “fine” at first and then become too strong as it accumulates over the next few days. When it’s done right, people often report they can finally focus on therapy, relationships, work, and the bigger recovery plan.
sections.clinical_details: Methadone is a long-acting opioid agonist used in structured OUD treatment. Clinical outcomes depend heavily on careful induction, appropriate dose titration, treatment retention, and wraparound services. In real life, the biggest risks cluster early: initiation, conversion from other opioids, and dose increases—because methadone’s peak respiratory depressant effects can lag behind the perceived effects.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Methadone can cause fatal overdose—especially during the first days of treatment, after dose increases, or when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, or other sedatives.
sections.black_box: Methadone exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur, especially during initiation or following a dose increase. Methadone can prolong the QT interval and cause dangerous arrhythmias (including torsades de pointes). Concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
other: Methadone accumulates: full effect on a dose may not be seen for 3 to 5 days—this is why fast titration can be deadly
QT prolongation risk: higher doses, electrolyte problems, liver impairment, and QT-prolonging meds increase risk
Accidental ingestion of even one dose (especially in children) can be fatal
Medication errors: oral solutions come in different concentrations—mixing up mg and mL can cause overdose and death
Pregnancy: neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) is expected and treatable, but can be life-threatening if not recognized and managed
Long-term opioid risks are now emphasized in FDA labeling updates (addiction, misuse, overdose, and harm from unsafe discontinuation), plus stronger interaction warnings including with gabapentinoids
patient_counseling: Do not mix methadone with alcohol. Don’t gamble with this—people die from this combination.
Tell your prescriber about every sedating medication you take (benzodiazepines, sleep meds, gabapentin/pregabalin, antihistamines, muscle relaxers).
If you feel unusually sleepy, confused, or your breathing feels slow/shallow—treat it as urgent. This can be overdose.
Use a real measuring device for liquid methadone. Never use kitchen spoons.
Store locked and out of reach. One accidental dose can be fatal for a child or opioid-naive adult.
If you stop or miss doses, your tolerance drops fast. Returning to an old dose can overdose you.
Ask about naloxone (or nalmefene) and keep it available—teach people close to you how to use it.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common problems are sedation, constipation, sweating, and nausea. The most dangerous problems are slowed breathing (overdose) and heart rhythm issues (QT prolongation). Side effects and risks increase when methadone is combined with other sedatives or titrated too quickly.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness, fatigue, or feeling “too calm” (especially early or after dose increases)
Constipation (very common and does not reliably improve over time)
Mood and thinking changes (foggy thinking, irritability, dysphoria in some people)

common.patient_note: Sedation is not just annoying—it can be a warning sign. If you’re getting visibly sleepy, nodding, or hard to wake (especially 2 to 4 hours after dosing), the dose may be too high or you may be combining methadone with something sedating.

Constipation is a top reason people hate opioids, and methadone is no exception. Plan for it early: hydration, fiber if tolerated, activity, and clinician-approved bowel regimens. Don’t wait until it becomes severe.
Nausea often shows up early and may settle as your body adjusts. If vomiting or dehydration happens, your dosing and safety plan may need reassessment.
Some people sweat a lot on methadone. It’s not dangerous by itself, but it can be uncomfortable and socially stressful.

Long-term opioid exposure can reduce sex hormones and impact libido, mood, energy, and bone health. If you feel flat, exhausted, or your sexual function changes, bring it up—this is a real medical issue, not a character flaw.

serious: Respiratory depression / overdose: slow, shallow breathing; extreme sleepiness; blue lips; unresponsiveness. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
QT prolongation and torsades de pointes: fainting, palpitations, sudden dizziness. EMERGENCY EVALUATION NEEDED.
Severe sedation from interactions (benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentinoids, sleep meds): can progress to coma/death.
Opioid withdrawal if abruptly reduced or stopped: agitation, anxiety, insomnia, GI distress, muscle aches; can be prolonged.
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia: pain sensitivity can worsen paradoxically; may require dose reduction or opioid rotation under expert care.
Hypoglycemia: uncommon but potentially serious—watch for sweating, shakiness, confusion, faintness (especially at higher doses or in people with diabetes risk factors).

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Methadone interactions can be life-threatening because they can either raise methadone levels (causing overdose) or disrupt heart rhythm (QT prolongation). The most dangerous interactions are with other CNS depressants.

items.with: Benzodiazepines (alprazolam, clonazepam, lorazepam) and other sedatives
items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death.
items.action: Avoid when possible. If there is no alternative, use the lowest effective doses, limit duration, and monitor closely. Visible sedation is a red flag—consider holding or adjusting dosing under medical supervision.
Do not drink alcohol while on methadone.

items.risk: Additive CNS and respiratory depression (risk is higher with higher doses, older age, sleep apnea, and other sedatives).
items.action: Use extreme caution; avoid stacking sedatives. Monitor for oversedation and breathing changes.

items.risk: Increased methadone levels → sedation and potentially fatal respiratory depression.
items.action: If an inhibitor is started, stopped, or dose-changed, reassess sedation/withdrawal and adjust methadone dosing carefully.

items.risk: Lower methadone levels → withdrawal, cravings, destabilization; stopping an inducer can then raise methadone levels and cause overdose.
items.action: Treat inducer changes as high-risk transitions. Monitor closely and adjust dosing cautiously.

items.risk: Additive QT prolongation → torsades de pointes risk.
items.action: Check QTc risk factors, correct electrolytes, and consider ECG monitoring when combining QT-prolonging meds.

items.risk: Can raise methadone levels in some people.
items.action: Avoid or use consistently with monitoring; report increased sedation.

items.with: Mixed agonist/antagonist opioids or partial agonists (e.g., buprenorphine started too early)
items.action: Transitions must be planned. For buprenorphine, methadone is often tapered to ~30 to 40 mg and held before a carefully timed induction.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping methadone abruptly can trigger a long, miserable withdrawal and can increase overdose risk if someone returns to opioids after losing tolerance. Tapering should be individualized, slow, and collaborative—especially in OUD, where stability and relapse prevention matter.
key_points: Methadone withdrawal can peak later and last longer than withdrawal from short-acting opioids.
Overdose risk rises after tapering or stopping: tolerance drops quickly, so going back to an old dose (or using illicit opioids) can be fatal.
OUD long-term discontinuation approach: often reduce by 5% to 10% every 1 to 2 weeks, with pauses if cravings or withdrawal break through.
If withdrawal symptoms flare, a common move is to return to the previous stable dose and then taper more slowly (smaller reductions or longer intervals).
Support matters: counseling, recovery supports, mental health treatment, and relapse prevention planning should be part of the taper—tapering is not just math.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Methadone dosing for opioid use disorder is highly individualized. The biggest safety rule: go slow. Methadone builds up over several days, so a dose that feels fine on day 1 can become too strong by day 3 to 5.

adult.oud_initial_low_or_no_tolerance: 2.5 to 10 mg PO as a single observed dose (use the low end when tolerance is uncertain or medical risk is higher)
adult.oud_initial_with_withdrawal_and_no_sedat: 20 to 30 mg PO as a single observed dose (maximum initial dose: 30 mg)
adult.oud_observation_and_additional_dose: Observe for 2 to 4 hours after the first dose; if withdrawal is not suppressed or returns, an additional 5 to 10 mg PO may be given; total day-1 dose should not exceed 40 mg
adult.oud_maintenance_typical_range: 60 to 120 mg PO daily (individualize to eliminate withdrawal for 24 hours, reduce cravings, and minimize sedation)
adult.oud_titration: Increase cautiously; many experts limit increases to ≤10 mg every 5 days, and go slower (e.g., 5 mg weekly) in lower-tolerance or higher-risk patients
adult.oud_split_dosing: If sedation occurs after dosing but withdrawal/cravings return before the next dose, consider divided dosing (e.g., twice daily) under clinician guidance
adult.oud_missed_doses: If >4 consecutive doses are missed, reassess and consider restarting at a lower dose with gradual re-titration due to reduced tolerance
adult.withdrawal_short_term_stabilization: Titrate to ~40 mg/day in divided doses to achieve stabilization; maintain ~40 mg/day for 2 to 3 days, then taper daily or every 2 days based on tolerance and setting
adult.rapid_initiation_hospital_only: Hospital-only protocols may use higher day-by-day dosing with addiction specialist oversight (avoid in older adults, QTc >500 ms, end-organ failure, benzodiazepine/alcohol use, or major interacting meds)

sections.simple_explanation: Methadone is long-acting and accumulates. That’s why the safest induction is slow and observed. The goal is steady: no withdrawal, reduced cravings, and no oversedation.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Methadone is commonly used in pregnancy for opioid use disorder because untreated OUD can be more dangerous than supervised treatment. Pregnancy and postpartum physiology can change methadone levels, and newborn monitoring is essential.
sections.pregnancy: Methadone crosses the placenta. For pregnant patients with OUD, opioid agonist treatment is recommended by major guidelines. Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS/NAS) is expected and treatable but can be life-threatening if not recognized and managed. As pregnancy progresses, methadone clearance may increase and the half-life may decrease, sometimes requiring dose adjustments or split dosing. Do not abruptly discontinue opioids during pregnancy; tapering, if appropriate, should be planned to minimize maternal withdrawal risk.
sections.lactation: Methadone is present in breast milk and infants can be exposed. Breastfeeding is often allowed and may help mitigate newborn withdrawal in OUD treatment when there are no contraindications (e.g., ongoing illicit substance use). Infants should be monitored for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, limpness, or breathing difficulty—especially during maternal dose titration or if methadone is started postpartum.
sections.geriatrics: Use extreme caution and start low. Older adults may be more sensitive to sedation, respiratory depression, falls, constipation, and delirium. For OUD treatment, lower initial oral doses (e.g., 10 to 20 mg) are commonly recommended in patients >60 years of age, with slow titration and close monitoring.
sections.hepatic: Use with caution. Methadone is hepatically metabolized and the half-life can be prolonged in severe liver impairment. In cirrhosis or significant hepatic dysfunction, use the lowest effective dose and titrate more gradually; monitor for oversedation and encephalopathy risk.
sections.renal: Methadone levels are not substantially altered in many patients with kidney impairment, but advanced kidney disease often comes with multiple comorbidities and higher interaction/QT risk. In severe renal impairment (e.g., CrCl ≤10 mL/min) or dialysis, some references recommend starting at 50% to 75% of typical doses and titrating gradually with close monitoring.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation and mental status (especially during initiation and dose changes): watch for nodding, confusion, slowed thinking, or being hard to arouse
Respiratory status: slow or shallow breathing, snoring/apnea, daytime sleepiness—risk rises with other sedatives, sleep apnea, COPD, and early titration
QTc monitoring (ECG): baseline ECG for patients with risk factors; repeat after initiation and after significant dose increases; reassess if syncope/palpitations occur
Electrolytes (when QT risk is present): potassium and magnesium, especially with vomiting/diuretics or other medical illness
Drug interactions: review changes in CYP inhibitors/inducers, QT-prolonging meds, and all CNS depressants (including gabapentinoids)
Misuse/diversion risk: early refills, lost medication reports, escalating dose requests, use of multiple prescribers, or continued use despite harm
Toxicology testing: baseline and periodic monitoring as clinically appropriate (especially in long-term treatment)
PDMP checks: baseline and periodically to reduce duplicate controlled prescriptions
In OUD treatment: monitor cravings, withdrawal breakthrough, illicit opioid use, and functional outcomes (housing, work, relationships, safety)
Infectious disease screening in OUD care: hepatitis and HIV testing per clinical guidance
Constipation plan: bowel regimen and monitoring for severe constipation or obstruction symptoms
Metabolic/endocrine symptoms: libido changes, fatigue, mood flattening, possible hypogonadism; consider glucose monitoring if symptoms suggest hypoglycemia or at higher doses

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Methadone comes in multiple oral and injectable forms. Liquid concentrations vary—this is a common source of dosing errors, so precise measuring and clear communication (mg vs mL) matter.
items: Tablets for oral suspension / dispersible: 40 mg (e.g., Diskets and equivalents; used in 10 mg increments when dispersed)
Oral solution: 5 mg/5 mL; 10 mg/5 mL
Oral concentrate: 10 mg/mL (high concentration—high error risk if mismeasured)
Injection solution: 10 mg/mL (IM/IV/SUBQ; typically inpatient use)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Methadone is a long-acting opioid agonist that activates opioid receptors in the brain and body. In OUD treatment, that steady receptor coverage prevents withdrawal and reduces cravings, which lowers the drive to use illicit opioids. Methadone also has NMDA receptor antagonism, which may contribute to its unique clinical effects and may matter in some pain and tolerance pathways. The same mechanism that stabilizes withdrawal can also slow breathing—especially if dosing is too high or combined with other sedatives.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Methadone is one of the core medications for opioid use disorder. It’s especially helpful for people who need strong withdrawal and craving control, who have not done well on other treatments, or who benefit from the structure of an opioid treatment program. It requires careful induction and monitoring because methadone accumulates and can cause delayed overdose. In many regions, outpatient OUD methadone is dispensed under strict regulations (often through certified programs), which is about safety as much as it is about policy.

seo.title: Methadone: Uses for Opioid Use Disorder, Dosing, Risks, QT Prolongation & Withdrawal
seo.description: Methadone for opioid use disorder: what it’s for, how dosing works, why it accumulates, major risks (overdose, QT prolongation), dangerous interactions with benzos/alcohol/gabapentin, naloxone safety, and tapering basics.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is methadone used for in psychiatry/addiction treatment?
faqs.a: Methadone is used to treat opioid use disorder (OUD). It prevents withdrawal, reduces cravings, and helps people stabilize so they can actually work on recovery (therapy, relationships, rebuilding life). It’s not a PRN medication and it’s not meant to make someone feel “high.”

Some people feel withdrawal relief within the first few hours, but the most important thing to know is that methadone accumulates. A dose can feel okay on day 1 and become too strong by day 3 to 5. That’s why safe induction is slow and carefully monitored.

faqs.q: Is methadone just replacing one addiction with another?
faqs.a: No. Dependence and addiction aren’t the same thing. Methadone can cause physical dependence (your body adapts), but addiction is about loss of control and harm. In OUD treatment, methadone is used in a structured way to reduce harm, prevent overdose, and support long-term functioning.

faqs.q: Why is methadone considered high-risk early on?
faqs.a: Because the peak breathing-suppression effects can hit later and last longer than the “felt” effects, especially when treatment is starting or doses are increasing. Methadone also builds up over days, so fast titration can unintentionally lead to overdose.

faqs.q: Can I take benzodiazepines or sleep meds with methadone?
faqs.a: This is one of the biggest danger zones. Combining methadone with benzodiazepines, alcohol, gabapentinoids, or other sedatives can cause fatal respiratory depression. If there’s truly no alternative, it requires the lowest effective doses, short duration, and close monitoring. Never combine on your own.

faqs.q: What is QT prolongation and why does methadone get ECG talk?
faqs.a: QT prolongation is a change on an EKG that can raise the risk of a dangerous arrhythmia (torsades de pointes). Methadone can prolong QT—risk increases with higher doses, electrolyte issues, liver problems, and QT-prolonging medications. If you have fainting, palpitations, or sudden dizziness, get evaluated urgently.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss methadone doses?
faqs.a: Missing doses can trigger withdrawal and destabilize recovery. But the other major issue is tolerance: if you miss multiple days and then return to your old dose, you can overdose because tolerance drops. If you’ve missed several doses, the safest move is reassessment and cautious re-titration.

faqs.q: Should I have naloxone if I’m on methadone?
faqs.a: Yes. Naloxone (and in some places nalmefene) is an opioid overdose reversal medication. It’s especially important if you have sleep apnea, use any sedatives, have a history of overdose, or have kids/other people in the home who could accidentally ingest medication. Teach people close to you how to use it.

Methadone is commonly used to treat OUD during pregnancy because untreated OUD can be very dangerous. Newborn withdrawal (NOWS/NAS) can occur and needs planning and monitoring, but it’s expected and treatable. Dosing may need adjustment during pregnancy and postpartum because the body changes how it processes methadone.

faqs.q: Can methadone help with anxiety and insomnia?
faqs.a: Methadone doesn’t treat primary anxiety or insomnia disorders. But if your anxiety, agitation, and insomnia are being driven by opioid withdrawal, stabilizing withdrawal can make those symptoms dramatically better. If anxiety persists after stabilization, that’s when you treat it as its own condition.

faqs.q: How do people taper off methadone safely?
faqs.a: Slowly and with a plan. A common long-term approach is reducing by about 5% to 10% every 1 to 2 weeks, with pauses when withdrawal or cravings break through. The taper schedule should match your goals and stability, and it should include relapse-prevention planning because overdose risk rises after tolerance drops.
